questions.q: State the exact constitutional articles that govern parliamentary privileges for (a) Parliament and (b) State Legislatures, and name the specific clause that grants immunity from legal proceedings for speeches and votes in the House.
questions.a: (a) Article 105 for Parliament; (b) Article 194 for State Legislatures. The immunity clause is Article 105(2) [and Article 194(2) for states]: "No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof." A wrong answer (e.g., citing Article 19 or Article 21) reveals confusion between fundamental rights of citizens and special institutional privileges of legislators — a category error between individual rights and institutional powers.

questions.q: Explain why the Constitution grants freedom of speech in Parliament (Article 105(1)) that is wider than the fundamental right to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a), and why this difference matters for legislative functioning.
questions.a: Article 105(1) grants absolute freedom of speech in Parliament "subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of Parliament" — but crucially NOT subject to Article 19(2) reasonable restrictions (public order, defamation, etc.). Article 19(1)(a) is subject to Article 19(2) restrictions. This difference matters because legislators must debate sensitive issues (corruption, security, policy failures) without fear of defamation suits or sedition charges. A wrong answer claiming "both are same" misses the constitutional design: legislative speech is functionally protected to ensure robust deliberation, while citizen speech is balanced against social interests.

questions.q: An MP makes a speech in Lok Sabha accusing a private businessman of tax evasion and money laundering, naming him directly. The businessman files a criminal defamation case in a district court. The MP claims parliamentary immunity under Article 105(2). As a legal advisor, analyze whether the immunity applies and what the court's likely response would be.
questions.a: Immunity under Article 105(2) applies fully. The MP cannot be sued in any court for "anything said" in Parliament. The Supreme Court in *Tej Kiran Jain v. Sanjiva Reddy* (1970) held that "anything said" covers all speech within the House, even if malicious or defamatory. The court will dismiss the case at the threshold. A wrong answer suggesting "immunity doesn't apply if speech is malicious" or "court can examine malice" reveals misunderstanding of the absolute nature of Article 105(2) — the Constitution deliberately chose absolute immunity to prevent judicial scrutiny of legislative speech.

questions.q: Compare the Searchlight case (1959) and the Keshav Singh case (1965) on the question: Can a High Court entertain a habeas corpus petition challenging a legislative assembly's order punishing a non-member for contempt/breach of privilege? What constitutional principle was at stake?
questions.a: In *Searchlight* (1959), the Supreme Court held that Article 194(3) privileges (then uncodified, based on House of Commons) are subject to fundamental rights — so courts could review. In *Keshav Singh* (1965), the UP Assembly arrested a non-member (Keshav Singh) for contempt; the Allahabad HC granted bail via habeas corpus. The Assembly then passed a resolution condemning the judges and ordering their arrest — creating a constitutional crisis. The Supreme Court ultimately held (by majority) that courts CAN entertain habeas corpus petitions against legislative detention orders because Article 21 (personal liberty) and Article 226 (writ jurisdiction) are not excluded by legislative privilege. The principle at stake: **legislative privilege is not above the Constitution** — especially fundamental rights and judicial review. A wrong answer claiming "legislature is supreme in privilege matters" misses the basic structure doctrine and the judiciary's role as guardian of the Constitution.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "Parliamentary privileges, especially the power to punish for contempt and breach of privilege, violate the principle of separation of powers because they allow the legislature to act as judge, prosecutor, and executioner in its own cause."
questions.a: The argument has merit but is constitutionally incomplete. True: the House acts as judge in its own cause (no external appeal traditionally), raising separation-of-powers concerns. However, the Constitution *expressly* grants this power under Articles 105(3) and 194(3) — it is a textual exception to strict separation, justified by functional necessity (protecting legislative dignity and authority). The Supreme Court has mitigated the concern by asserting judicial review over *mala fide* or *perverse* privilege actions (*Keshav Singh*, *Raja Ram Pal* 2007). A one-sided answer calling it "unconstitutional" ignores the constitutional text; an answer calling it "fully valid" ignores judicial checks. The nuanced evaluation: it's a *constitutional accommodation* with built-in judicial safeguards, not a separation-of-powers violation per se.

questions.q: Draft a constitutional amendment proposal (2-3 clauses) that would codify parliamentary privileges in a statute while preserving legislative independence, addressing the current gap where privileges are defined by "House of Commons as on 26 January 1950" under Article 105(3). Justify each clause.
questions.a:
**Proposed Amendment to Article 105:**
*Clause 1:* Replace Article 105(3) with: "The powers, privileges, and immunities of each House of Parliament and of its members and committees shall be such as are defined by Parliament by law, and until so defined, shall be those existing on the commencement of this Constitution." — *Justification:* Ends reliance on foreign precedent (House of Commons 1950), fulfills the Constitution's own mandate for codification.
*Clause 2:* Add new Article 105(4): "No law made under clause (3) shall abridge the freedom of speech guaranteed under clause (1) or the immunity under clause (2), nor shall it authorize punishment exceeding [specified limits] without judicial review." — *Justification:* Entrenches core immunities, subjects penal powers to judicial scrutiny.
*Clause 3:* Add: "Any person aggrieved by a decision of a House under privilege law may appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds of violation of fundamental rights or jurisdictional error." — *Justification:* Creates appellate safeguard without undermining House authority. A poor answer merely says "make a law" without addressing the tension between codification and legislative autonomy, or fails to protect Article 105(1)/(2) core.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ privileges are special rights, immunities, and exemptions enjoyed by each House of Parliament and its members collectively and individually under Article 105 of the Constitution, enabling them to discharge their legislative functions without fear, interference, or legal obstruction.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you watch a heated Lok Sabha debate where an MP makes serious allegations ______ a corporate house.
What is Parliamentary privileges? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Parliamentary privileges are special rights, immunities, and exemptions enjoyed by each House of Parliament and its members collectively and individually under Article 105 of the Constitution, enabling them to discharge their legislative functions without fear, interference, or legal obstruction.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Parliamentary privileges are special rights, immunities, and exemptions enjoyed by each House of Parliament and its members collectively and individually under Article ______ of the Constitution, enabling them to discharge their legislative functions without fear, interference, or legal obstruction.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Parliamentary privileges?
questions.a: Students often believe parliamentary privilege means "MPs are above the law" or "MPs cannot be arrested for any crime." The precise error: confusing *immunity from civil arrest during session* (Article 105, Section 135A CrPC) with *immunity from criminal prosecution*.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can distinguish between collective privileges (House as a body) and individual privileges (member), explain the constitutional basis (Articles 105 and 194), analyze the tension between parliamentary privilege and fundamental rights (Article 19), and evaluate landmark cases like the Searchlight case (1959) and Keshav Singh case.
